generation.hypothesis: The addition of Cr, Al, and Si elements to refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) can improve their high-temperature oxidation resistance by forming a dense oxidation film on the surface of the alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) with a nominal composition of Mo, Nb, Ta, and W, and possibly other elements such as Ti, Cr, V, Si, and Al.
generation.intervention: Addition of Cr, Al, and Si elements to the RHEA composition.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a dense oxidation film on the surface of the alloy.
generation.mechanism: The added elements (Cr, Al, and Si) react with oxygen to form a protective oxide scale, reducing the oxidation rate of the alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved high-temperature oxidation resistance of the RHEA, potentially leading to increased service life and reliability in high-temperature applications.
generation.baseline: RHEAs without the added Cr, Al, and Si elements, which are known to have poor oxidation resistance.
generation.boundary: The optimal composition and amount of added elements (Cr, Al, and Si) to achieve improved oxidation resistance without compromising mechanical properties.
generation.uncertainty: The exact mechanism of oxidation resistance improvement, the optimal composition and amount of added elements, and the potential trade-offs with mechanical properties.

falsification_experiment.design: High-temperature oxidation test of RHEA samples with and without added Cr, Al, and Si elements.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxidation rate and scale thickness of the RHEA samples with added Cr, Al, and Si elements are not significantly lower than those of the samples without added elements, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) first appeared in public view in 2010 [ [1] ]. Thereafter, they aroused great concern from researchers at home and abroad. Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. RHEAs, with excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, are considered promising high-temperature application materials, which are suitable for complex working conditions such as atomic energy, aerospace, the military industry, advanced nuclear reactors, etc. Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [7] , [8] , [9] ]. Recently the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), consisting of four or more principle metallic elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios, has attracted considerable interest owing to its tendency to form solid solution with outstanding mechanical and functional properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

Since the first WMoTaNb RHEA was reported in 2010, many literatures have been focused on the preparation methods and mechanical properties of RHEAs [ [7] , [8] ]. For example, the BCC WMoTaNb and WMoTaNbV HEAs maintained yield strength of 405 and 477 MPa at 1600 °C respectively, which were much higher than that of Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [9] ].
